talks.title: Who Can You Trust w/ Evan Francen and Michael Kennedy
talks.teaser: Examines who Can You Trust w/ Evan Francen and Michael Kennedy and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Building Trust in Security Services

Evan Francen (FRSecure) and Michael Kennedy (Ostra Cyber) discuss earning reputations as trustworthy advisors. FRSecure’s rule: never sell unneeded services; Ostra formed after seeing small businesses treat ransomware as inevitable rather than addressable.

Industry Overwhelm

They describe long hours, passion-driven overwork, imposter syndrome, and mental-health strain common among practitioners. Work-life balance, they suggest, should be judged by relationship health rather than arbitrary hour counts.

Honesty Over Hype

Both founders say they regularly tell prospects when they are not the right fit, redirecting them elsewhere. Truth-telling is framed as a core value partners must hold them accountable to maintain.

Conversation Style

The session is informal—microphone issues, ADHD tangents, and audience karaoke jokes—but centers on integrity, burnout, and fixing broken incentives in cybersecurity marketing and consulting.

talks.title: Defensive Evasion: Detecting the Threat Actor's Playbook w/ Max Rogers
talks.teaser: Discusses defensive Evasion: Detecting the Threat Actors Playbook w/ Max Rogers and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Max Rogers, Director of the Threat Operations Center at Huntress and former incident responder at Mandiant and FireEye, explores defense evasion techniques observed across small-to-midsize business (SMB) intrusions. Drawing on real-world telemetry from over 1.6 million endpoints and four to ten hands-on keyboard intrusions weekly, Rogers analyzes how modern threat actors navigate the MITRE ATT&CK framework. He exposes the sharp dichotomy between evading automated security tooling versus evading human analysts, providing detection engineers with practical strategies to catch attackers during lateral movement and privilege abuse.

Key Topics:
- Evolution of threat models: Cyber Kill Chain vs. Mandiant Lifecycle vs. MITRE ATT&CK
- Deconstructing Defense Evasion (TA0005): evading automated tooling ("the WHAT") vs. human analysts ("the WHO")
- Threat actor mindset: flagrant, unabashed disregard for human detection during ransomware operations
- Multi-telemetry resilience, hunting hands-on lateral movement, and contributing to open-source Sigma rules

Technical Details:
Rogers contextualizes defense evasion within the evolution of cybersecurity frameworks, tracking the progression from the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain to the Mandiant Threat Actor Lifecycle and the MITRE ATT&CK matrix. While early frameworks focused on perimeter intrusion and long-term espionage dwell times, MITRE ATT&CK provides granular sub-techniques covering the entire tactical progression. Rogers focuses on Defense Evasion (TA0005), emphasizing an essential distinction often overlooked by defenders: the difference between evading automated technology ("the WHAT", such as AV, EDR, network proxies, and DNS filters) and evading human defenders ("the WHO", such as SOC analysts, threat hunters, and system administrators).

In the mid-market and SMB space, where attackers aim to deploy ransomware within days rather than conduct prolonged cyber espionage, threat actors exhibit a blatant, unabashed disregard for human detection. They do not craft subtle, low-and-slow bypasses; instead, they aggressively attack security software. Telemetry from Huntress shows attackers routinely issuing commands to disable Windows Defender (using PowerShell commands like Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath), attempting to stop EDR services, clearing Windows event logs with wevtutil, and running noisy Living Off the Land Binaries (LOLBins). Attackers operate under the assumption that if they successfully terminate or blind the automated endpoint sensors, there will be no human analyst monitoring the environment to stop them from encrypting systems.

To defeat these tactics, Rogers stresses the necessity of maintaining dual, independent sources of telemetry. An attacker can rarely disable multiple disparate defensive sensors simultaneously with a single command. By deploying independent antivirus and EDR agents, or forwarding raw event logs directly off-box to a centralized SIEM, defenders ensure that actions taken to disable one product trigger immediate high-priority alerts in the secondary system. Furthermore, Rogers emphasizes that while automated prevention tools excel at stopping initial commodity phishing payloads, human detection engineering and threat hunting must focus on hands-on keyboard behaviors in the middle of the MITRE ATT&CK matrix—specifically credential dumping, internal reconnaissance, and lateral movement.

Key Takeaways:
Security operations teams must recognize that ransomware operators prioritize blinding automated security software over avoiding human scrutiny. Organizations must deploy redundant, decoupled telemetry layers (such as EDR combined with independent off-box log collection) to ensure that tampering attempts against endpoint agents generate immediate alerts. Threat hunting teams should focus detection engineering efforts on hands-on keyboard activities—such as service disabling, defensive exclusions, and lateral movement—while sharing community detection logic through open-source projects like Sigma.

talks.title: Weathering the Storm: How We Can Turn the Tide on Threats (Panel)
talks.teaser: Discusses weathering the Storm: how organizations can Turn the Tide on Threats (Panel) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Panel focus

Weathering the Storm at Hacks and Hops gathers Judy Hatchet (Surescripts CISO), Martin Holste (Trellix cloud CTO), Eric Hansen and Seth Bowling (FRSecure offensive/R&D) to discuss turning the tide on threats.

Program foundations

Panelists debate starting points—budget and outsourcing vs. hiring, policies/standards as governance baseline, SOC readiness, and asset inventory as prerequisites to securing what you own.

Frameworks

Judy notes frameworks (NIST CSF, HITRUST, COBIT) provide guardrails and maturity benchmarking but do not alone measure policy adherence or culture; they complement—not replace—standards work.

Where orgs fail

Discussion shifts to misallocated security dollars, compliance-driven misprioritization, and whether clients should fear zero-days more than absent programs—consensus favors fundamentals over headline O-days alone.

talks.title: Dissecting the Ransomware Kill Chain w/ Oscar Minks
talks.teaser: Outlines dissecting the Ransomware Kill Chain w/ Oscar Minks and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Ransomware's Human Cost

Oscar Minks, CTO at FRSecure, frames ransomware through victim impact: average recovery downtime exceeds 21 days, a duration most small businesses cannot survive. Global costs reached roughly $20 billion in 2021, up from $5 billion in 2017, with every sector targeted regardless of perceived value.

## Mapping the Kill Chain

Minks walks through attacker reconnaissance mirroring red-team methodology: enumerating domains and subdomains for look-alike phishing sites, scanning external IP space and ASNs, identifying open services, and harvesting leaked credentials from breach dumps and projects like Project Hifi.

## Pre-Attack Intelligence Gathering

Before payload delivery, adversaries study organizational structure, technology stack, and credential exposure. Leaked corporate credentials remain a primary entry vector, often available at scale through underground markets and public breach collections.

## Defensive Takeaways

Understanding each kill-chain stage enables proportional controls: domain monitoring for typosquats, external attack-surface management, credential rotation after third-party leaks, and recovery planning that assumes multi-week outages. Minks emphasizes that good people and small co-ops deserve the same rigor as large enterprises.
